title: What Size Dehumidifier Do I Need? Sizing Chart & Calculator
h1: What Size Dehumidifier Do You Need?
dek: Square footage is only half the answer. Here’s how to match pints to your space — and how dampness changes everything.
description: What size dehumidifier do I need? Use our dehumidifier size chart by square footage and dampness, a quick calculator, and the 2019 DOE rating change explained.
intro: **What size dehumidifier do I need?** It’s the first question nearly every shopper asks, and the honest answer depends on two things: how big the space is and how damp it really is. A 1,000-square-foot basement that just smells a little musty needs far less capacity than the same basement with water seeping through the walls after every storm.

There’s a second trap, too. In 2019 the Department of Energy changed how dehumidifiers are rated, and every number on the box dropped — even though the machines didn’t get any weaker. Compare an old “70-pint” unit to a new “50-pint” and you may be looking at nearly the same capacity.
Below you’ll find a sizing chart that combines square footage and dampness, a simple calculator you can do in your head and the adjustments that charts usually leave out.

blocks.title: Past what a portable can handle
blocks.text: Flood cleanup, standing water on a slab or a crawl space that seeps after every rain calls for an industrial-size LGR dehumidifier. See our [best commercial dehumidifier](/best/best-commercial-dehumidifier/) picks.

items: **Measure the space.** Multiply length by width. Add connected rooms if there’s no door between them.
**Rate the dampness.** Musty only = moderately damp. Beading on walls or windows = very damp. Seepage or puddles = wet.
**Read the chart.** Find your row and column above.
**Adjust for ceilings.** If ceilings are higher than 8 feet, move up one tier.
**Adjust for moisture sources.** A laundry room, hot tub or shower nearby? Move up one tier.
**Between sizes?** Choose the larger one, as long as it has a humidistat that switches off at your target.

blocks.text: Example: a 1,200-square-foot basement with condensation on the foundation walls lands at 30–40 pints. With a dryer venting into the space, move up to a 50-pint unit.

blocks.text: Mid-size electric minis such as the Eva-Dry EDV-2400 add a built-in humidistat but remove only a small amount of water — fine for a closet or bathroom, not a bedroom. For whole-home systems, size by square footage and duct capacity instead; see our [best whole-house dehumidifier](/best/best-whole-house-dehumidifier/) guide.

Starting in June 2019, the DOE moved its official test from an 80°F room to a 65°F room to better reflect real basements. Cooler air holds less water, so every model’s rated capacity dropped — the hardware didn’t change, only the label.

blocks.text: Some brands still headline capacity under hot, saturated conditions (often 95°F and 90% humidity or more), which inflates the number further. Always compare DOE to DOE. For the mechanics behind those ratings, see [how does a dehumidifier work](/guides/how-does-a-dehumidifier-work/).

sections.heading: How to size a dehumidifier: the adjustments charts miss

items.label: Ceiling height
items.text: Charts assume 8-foot ceilings. Vaulted rooms hold more air per square foot, so size up a tier.

items.label: Open floor plans
items.text: Treat connected spaces as one area. A unit can’t dry only the room it sits in when there’s no door.

items.label: Temperature
items.text: Below about 60°F, compressor units remove less water; below about 41°F they start icing. Cold spaces need extra capacity or a desiccant.

items.label: Placement
items.text: A correctly sized unit jammed into a corner underperforms. Follow our [where to place a dehumidifier](/guides/where-to-place-a-dehumidifier/) rules.

items.label: Grow tents
items.text: Plant count and growth stage matter more than floor area. See our [best dehumidifier for grow tent](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-grow-tent/) guide.

blocks.text: Decide how damp the space is before you look at square footage — the same 1,000-square-foot room can need anywhere from 20 to 40 pints. Compare current DOE ratings, adjust for ceilings and moisture sources and, if you’re between sizes, choose the larger unit with a good humidistat. Then set that humidistat to around 45–50%; our [humidistat settings guide](/guides/dehumidifier-humidistat-settings-guide/) explains why.

faqs.q: What size dehumidifier do I need for a 1,000 sq ft basement?
faqs.a: About 20–25 pints (DOE 2019) if it’s moderately damp, 25–30 pints if you see condensation and 30–40 pints if there’s seepage or standing water. See our [best dehumidifier for 1,000 sq ft](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-1000-sq-ft/) picks.

faqs.q: What size dehumidifier do I need for 2,000 square feet?
faqs.a: Usually 30–50 pints depending on dampness, or a ducted whole-home unit if the space is spread across multiple rooms. Our [best dehumidifier for 2,000 sq ft](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-2000-sq-ft/) guide has specific picks.

faqs.q: Is it better to size up or down on a dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Size up one step if you’re between two sizes. A slightly larger unit with a humidistat reaches the target and cycles off. Avoid jumping several sizes, which adds cost without benefit.

faqs.q: Why is a new dehumidifier’s pint rating lower than my old one?
faqs.a: The DOE changed its test in 2019 from 80°F to 65°F. The same machine now earns a lower number — an old 70-pint unit is roughly a 50-pint unit today.

faqs.q: How do I know if my space is damp, very damp or wet?
faqs.a: Damp: a musty smell but no visible moisture. Very damp: beading on windows, pipes or walls. Wet: visible seepage or standing water. A hygrometer reading above 60% confirms a problem.

faqs.q: When do I need an industrial-size dehumidifier?
faqs.a: For flood cleanup, standing water, large warehouses or crawl spaces with constant seepage. Commercial LGR units are built to run continuously and pull moisture at lower humidity levels.
